https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/scie.text: Earlier this month, an Embraer 170 took off from Seattle in the US, flew over the Pacific, landed in Alaska and flew back, completing a four-hour round trip over open ocean, a fairly regular flight except for one key detail â it flew without GPS.Now, pilots are not entirely lost without GPS; they have other ânav aidsâ such as charts, maps, beacons and air-traffic control. They can also rely on visual references like monuments, hills, rivers and other terrain features to find the right airport.But the Embraer in this case had flown over featureless ocean. So without satellite positioning or monuments to go by, how did the pilots know their position? On board was a piece of tech many countries, including ours, have been racing to perfect, called quantum navigation. It uses minutely sensitive quantum sensors to read variations in the Earthâs magnetic field (caused largely by magnetised rock underground) and compares them with an onboard magnetic map. By matching the patterns, and combining the data with inputs from gyroscopes and accelerometers, the aircraft can determine its position even without GPS.The Sept 4 Embraer test was the first publicly reported long-duration, open-sea demonstration of one variant of quantum navigation, using a conventional plane with no cockpit retrofits.The test was a success; the technology proved 89% more accurate than the ânav aidsâ pilots use if GPS fails. Itâs an important development, especially if one considers what happened in March 2024 to UK defence secretary Grant Shappsâs plane, near Russiaâs Kaliningrad. For 30 minutes, Shappsâs jet had no GPS or onboard internet, suggesting satellite signals to it were being jammed. A month later, two airliners over Estonia had to abort landings after pilots noticed GPS interference. The next year, a plane carrying Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, had to circle a Bulgarian airport for an hour after it experienced similar glitches. Ships have been hit too. Between 2016 and 2018, over 1,000 commercial vessels saw their GPS being âspoofedâ or fed false location data.The cases have alarmed experts who now believe global satellite navigation is under sustained attack, an unsurprising inference given how easy it is to jam GPS signals â they have the strength of a âwhisperâ by the time they reach the ground.The Embraer that flew without a satellite signal bypasses these flaws in GPS. It showed that in the future, if satellites were to be knocked out of the sky, a plane would still be able to find its way. Later this year, US military is set to test quantum navigation on a much bigger plane, a C-17 transporter. tnn

Share Add a comment This photo illustration shows the Temu app in the App Store reflected in videos of Shein consumers, in Washington, DC, on February 23, 2023. (Photo by Stefani Reynolds / AFP) Add The Local as a preferred source Customers in Germany ordering products from outside the EU will soon face an additional processing fee of €2 per item category - in addition to the EU's new €3 customs duty. A new 'handling fee' of €2 will apply to items valued at less than €150 and ordered online from non-EU sites, starting on November 1st, 2026, as part of a new EU rule. The fee - which is in addition to an existing €3 EU tax on small packages - is meant to cover the increasing customs costs associated with the sheer volume of individual small packages coming into the bloc. It means that the total fees on packages from outside the EU will be €5 - although gifts are exempt. The fee is intended to target Chinese companies like Temu and Shein, but will also affect people who live in Germany and shop on sites based in countries outside the EU, including the UK, US and Canada. Advertisement In 2024, an estimated 4.6 billion low-value shipments were imported into the EU, nearly double compared to 2023, according to EU data. China accounted for about 91 per cent of them. The introduction of the €2 processing fee is the latest in a string of updates to EU regulations that are designed to limit imports of cheap products from companies such as Shein and Temu. On July 1st 2026, a €3 duty was applied to all goods valued at €150 or less and ordered online from sites outside of Europe. The introduction of an additional €2 handling fee will bring the total cost of importing an item to €5, suggesting further reductions in imports are in sight. Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from Germany How it works Both the €3 duty and the €2 handling fee apply to each category of item ordered. So for example, if you order three jumpers, the tax will only be €5 for the whole order. But if you buy one jumper and one pair of trousers, you'll be charged €10 for the parcel - €5 for the jumper and €5 for the trousers. In theory, these costs will be paid by the seller, whether that's an individual company or a marketplace platform such as Amazon. So customers shouldn't be getting an extra bill, or be charged by delivery companies when items arrive. But in practice, the seller could add this tax onto the price of their products. READ ALSO: Everything that changes in Germany in November 2026 Advertisement Loopholes Media reports suggest that some of the platforms targeted by these measures have already found a way to minimise the additional costs. Shein, which has opened a giant warehouse in Poland, now invites European shoppers to explore its "EU Warehouse" via its homepage. Temu, meanwhile, encourages consumers in Europe to visit the "Local Warehouse" section of the site , which includes product ranges stored at a giant warehouse in the Netherlands. Because these warehouses are located within EU borders, they're exempt from the fees. More changes to come Whilst the new €2 handling fee is set to remain, the €3 customs duty introduced in July is only a temporary measure. That doesn't mean it's going away, however. It will remain in place until 2028, when the EU Customs Data Hub in 2028 is set to open. At that point, all goods entering the EU will be subject to customs duty at the regular tariff for each product. EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said previously: “Our work to modernise how we manage trade at our borders is well on track, and we are close to completing the most ambitious customs reform since the creation of the Customs Union in 1968… With e-commerce expanding rapidly, the world is changing fast - and we need the right tools to keep pace.” Become a member or log in to continue reading More #Money #European Union #Living in Germany Comments Join the conversation in our comments section below.
